identity.title: Inhaled biologics: A paradigm shift in drug delivery for proteins, vaccines, and gene-based therapeutics.

content.abstract: Pulmonary drug delivery has emerged as a promising platform for the administration of biologics, offering direct access to the respiratory tract while minimising systemic exposure and associated adverse effects. Recent advances in inhalation technologies, formulation engineering, and carrier systems have significantly expanded the scope of inhaled biologics beyond conventional therapies. This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging inhaled biologics, including proteins, peptides, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapies, mRNA therapeutics, siRNA, CRISPR-based systems, vaccines, and nanocarrier-enabled delivery platforms. Key physiological barriers to pulmonary delivery, such as mucociliary clearance, alveolar macrophage uptake, mucus penetration, and epithelial transport, are critically discussed along with contemporary strategies to overcome these challenges. Recent developments in lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, exosomes, and inhalable dry powder systems are highlighted for their role in enhancing stability, targeting efficiency, and therapeutic outcomes. The review also examines clinical translation, regulatory considerations, aerosol performance, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships, and the integration of artificial intelligence in formulation design and precision delivery. Marketed inhaled biologics remain limited to a few products, including inhaled insulin. In contrast, most inhaled monoclonal antibodies, gene-based therapies, gene-editing approaches, and pulmonary vaccine platforms remain investigational, with evidence derived primarily from clinical studies at different stages or from preclinical models. This review distinguishes marketed products from clinical-stage candidates and preclinical proof-of-concept studies to clarify the current state of pulmonary biologic delivery.
